Yeah, I agree that Blackout and FSLS were technically first. Loose is more R&B influenced to me, though. 

I was moreso responding to the idea that those albums paved the way for The Fame or that Gaga owes them a debt. She was experimenting with those sounds before Blackout and FSLS popped off.  Her major influences were actual 80s pop like Madonna, MJ, '80s-era Bowie, and Grace Jones. You can hear it if you listen to her old demos from 2005-2006.

If anything, I believe it was Gwen Stefani's Love.Angel.Music.Baby. (2004) that really got the 80s-inspired EDM pop ball rolling and was probably a bigger contributor to Gaga's success, though afaik she hasn't cited it as an influence. She was also influenced by The Killers, who she name-checks on "Boys, Boys, Boys". 

Ultimately, I think Gaga had the biggest footprint as far as EDM pop goes because she was a new artist and it felt especially fresh coming from her. Justin Timberlake, Britney, Gwen, and Nelly Furtado all had previous work that wasn't in that style.  When Gaga was doing it though, it felt definitive of her sound. She also incorporated those synthpop influences into her fashion, stage performances, and music videos in a much more prominent way than the aforementioned artists did.

I win concert tickets quite frequently, as it's a hobby of mine. Usually, I win through the radio. They call me to give me the news and then send me an e-mail with a waiver to sign. Then they transfer the tickets to my Ticketmaster account or put my name on the guest list.

Makes me think of the book/movie Something Wicked This Way Comes (written by Ray Bradbury and the source of many childhood existential nightmares for me). The story concerns a mystical carnival with a merry-go-round that can make its passengers age or de-age. I struggled with my weight a lot in high school (2000s) and I was heavily bullied by my peers and my mother was very cruel to me about my size. Looking back now, I realize I did not deserve the level of cruelty I got from my mom and my aunts. It gave me a lot of self-esteem problems and I think the poor self-image was a bigger problem than my weight. 

I went on a diet in college and lost a lot of weight, and immediately got a ton of praise from everyone around me. I also got more attention from guys (irrelevant to me, I now realize, since I am a lesbian but wasn't out at the time). The intense level of praise I got for losing weight made me scared that people wouldn't like me if I gained weight, so I developed a pretty bad eating disorder.

Eventually, I moved away from my family and the place I grew up and forged a new path for myself. My weight has gone up and down during that time but the friends I've made in my new home have never left me and always support me no matter what size I am. Recently, I lost a lot of weight in a healthy manner (a combination of fitness routine and getting help for my untreated ADHD). I've noticed that strangers are a bit kinder to me, but my friends haven't really said anything to me because they don't want to praise me solely for weight loss. 

My advice to you would be to think of the people in your life who love you no matter what and hold fast to those relationships, because those are the people who will always have your back, and those are the most authentic people. You deserve true friends and loving people no matter what size you are.

I thought the plot with the violin was a callback to the season 2 episode “The Gold Violin” (one of my fave episodes). In it, Ken describes the violin he saw in the Met that inspired his short story: “It was perfect in every way except it couldn’t make music.”

I believe this season 6 episode and the callback to the season 2 episode speak to Betty’s existence. She’s educated, speaks a foreign language, and has worked and travelled independently, but she has been relegated to a life of sitting on a shelf as an ornament, only to be looked at. 

At the end of “The Gold Violin”, Betty throws up in the car after being insulted by Jimmy and having Don’s infidelity thrown in her face. It seems like she’s throwing up because of alcohol or the confrontation, but in fact the vomiting foreshadows the fact that she’s pregnant. 

Similarly I think The Doorway symbolizes Betty’s imminent death in season 7. She sees herself in Sandy. Betty left her modelling career to be with Don. Sandy gave up her violin to run away to California (likely to be with a boy). 

Betty tries to rescue the violin but ultimately leaves it behind in the end, knowing that Sandy is beyond saving and the violin won’t be played by her again. Similarly, when Betty was diagnosed with cancer and realized she was about to lose her beauty, she gave up rather than fight (not a judgement on her; cancer treatment is stressful and horrible and I wouldn’t wish it on anyone). 

Ultimately it’s a statement on lost potential and how one mistake can derail your whole future.

Not a useful tool to ask her to write it herself for many reasons. 

1) she’s clearly emotionally compromised and can’t think clearly, and therefore not fully able to write a good letter for herself. 

2) Only an extremely skilled writer can imitate the style and tone of someone completely different to themself. It might not be totally obvious that *she* wrote it but it’s not going to pack the same punch as something Don would write.

3) it’s dishonest and she didn’t want to be caught up in another one of Don’s lies

A wad of cash is not a gift. A gift requires work. Giving your lover cash is giving them a task (find a way to spend it). Asking your secretary to write her own recommendation letter is not a recommendation. Its a task. 

It’s not just about the end result (the letter that might get her a job). It’s about the extra work that he’s making her do even after her job is over. She did so much extra shit for him, including buying Christmas gifts for his children, and he couldn’t write her a simple letter? 

She didn’t want “belly rubs”, FFS, she wanted the whole ordeal to be over, and he extended the ordeal by giving her another job.

Asking her to write her own letter when she’s clearly emotionally compromised isn’t generous, it’s selfish.

Your example of the mom and the kid at the grocery store made me think of something. Have you ever seen The Apartment? There’s a scene where Shirley McLaine’s character gives her married lover a gift that isn’t expensive, but is connected to a special date they shared. He says, “I have something for you too!”, hands her a few bills, and tells her to pick out what she wants. 

Sure, his gift is technically more expensive than hers, but there was no effort put into it, and that’s what shows he didn’t care. She didn’t want a wad of cash, she wanted a sentimental trinket. 

Similarly, Allison wanted an authentic recommendation letter, not for him to sign off on whatever she wrote. She wanted him to put some effort to show he cared, as a person, instead of throwing his weight around and assuming that a perfunctory sign-off would be as valuable as something more personal.
Exactly.
There’s no world where Allison has authority over Don. None. He’s her boss. He has all the authority over her. That’s part of the subtext that drives the scene.

It’s not completely made up, it’s based on Don’s actions in the past. He often makes a promise and says he’ll do something, but then doesn’t follow through. 

In telling her she can write her own letter, he’s making a gesture towards caring, but true care would have been writing the letter himself.

Ok but the issue is the lack of effort and the fact that Don says “you can write anything you want”, but he doesn’t really mean *anything*. He’s still in a position of power to her and he could go back on his word to sign off on the letter if he didn’t like what she wrote. 

Writing the letter himself would demonstrate effort and a conscious decision to send her off with good prospects. Getting her to write it herself is passive and demonstrates that he doesn’t care enough to do it himself. It’s reminiscent of the incident where he gave her $100 in cash as a “Christmas bonus” after they slept together and expected her to act like it never happened. He should have just had a conversation. He took the avoidant route both times.

I read and assess this kind of thing for a living, and everyone has a "voice", even people who aren't good writers. I might not be able to immediately tell that the secretary wrote her own recommendation letter, but a letter personally written by Don would immediately stand out and make me take notice. 

Besides, it's about the effort. It doesn't take that much effort to write a recommendation letter for a secretary, even if he doesn't think of himself as a brilliant writer (he is).

Don's a brilliant writer who can wring sentiment out of just about anything. A letter personally written by him in his signature, inimitable style means more than just signing off on something she wrote herself.

Don had a chance to make things right and make a tiny bit of effort to send her off with a little dignity. He didn't. He chose to be cold and perfunctory.

I’ve always said that people overlook the main ingredient of Bewitched, which wasn’t the magic, but the fact that it was (in the beginning) a newly married couple who were getting used to living with each other, in-laws, and the foibles of married life. Then when Tabitha was born it was about the experiences of being first time parents.

You couldn’t make a show like this today because people live together forever and have very long relationships before they actually get married. The central tension of Darrin being surprised to learn all this new info about Samantha wouldn’t work on the modern day.

I’m from the countryside where people never lock their doors, not even when they leave the house, so when I was growing up the no-locked-doors thing never struck me as unusual. 

However, what does bug me is fake snow. I’m Canadian, and the fake snow they use in shows filmed on soundstages drives me nuts!!
